**MELI research for the 2026-11-20 paper-trading journal**

I ran 8 searches and opened 6 pages. The Zacks page was blocked by a bot check, so it doesn't count. The company's own release was not readable: the Finviz copy only points to the shareholder letter. Q3 figures therefore come from secondary write-ups (TIKR, Trefis, StockStory, Rio Times).

**The story**
- **What was reported.** Q3 was reported Nov 4 after the close. Revenue was $10.75B, up 45% (41% FX-neutral), with GMV up 33%, TPV up 51% and credit portfolio up 62% to about $18B. EPS of $8.83 missed consensus of about $9.27 (Trefis says $9.41). Operating margin was 6.3% versus 9.8% a year earlier. Operating income was $676M, down about 6%.
- **Why margin fell.** Management cited:
  - a lower free-shipping threshold and higher net shipping costs;
  - about 20% more fulfillment space ahead of peak season;
  - affiliate marketing in Brazil, where affiliate orders were up 240%;
  - higher energy and transport costs.
- **No guidance.** The CEO said they "accepted a lower margin." The CFO gave no margin target and said part of the capacity cost may reverse in Q4 as volume fills it. Recovery is described as gradual.
- **Reaction.** The stock fell 12% on Nov 5 to $1,530, a one-year low. The S&P 500 was reported down 4.4% that day (Trefis), so part of the drop was market-wide. It has kept sliding since. It is down about 20% from Oct 5 to Nov 10, and about 29-34% over twelve months.
- **Analysts.** Goldman kept Buy but cut its target to $2,100 on Nov 11. Consensus target is about $2,244 across 26 analysts, with a range of $1,750 to $2,800. Citi and UBS reportedly went neutral on margin doubts (the dates were not clear). The 2026 EPS estimate has fallen from $66.55 (Sept 2025) to $37.37, and the 2027 estimate is $54.44.
- **Valuation.** The stock trades at about 33x forward earnings, near its five-year low of about 30x and about half the five-year average of 62x. The cheapness is the bull case. The bear case is that margin recovery has already been pushed back once.
- **Credit.** Loans 15-90 days overdue were 7.0% of the portfolio, which is growing 62%. Nu Holdings, a Brazilian digital bank, reported Nov 12 with its 90+ day NPL ratio up to 7.3% from 6.9%. Its credit growth slowed to 33%. Brazilian consumer credit is a sector worry.
- **Competition.** Shopee is expanding in Brazil with four-hour delivery, new distribution centers and R$48M in Black Friday coupons. Amazon and Shopee are both pushing in Brazil. Mercado Livre responded with 24-month interest-free instalments and over R$100M in coupons, and is testing one-hour delivery.
- **Macro.** Brazil's presidential runoff caused an 11% drop in late October (StockStory). Wall Street has been weak, with the S&P 500 down five sessions through Nov 18. AI stocks have been jittery around Nvidia's earnings, and Nasdaq rose 0.4% on Nov 18. I found no company-specific news for Nov 19-20.

**What could move it over the next 1-10 sessions**
- **Upside:**
  - an oversold bounce from RSI 26, near the 52-week low;
  - a broad market recovery;
  - Black Friday (Nov 27) and Cyber Monday sales datapoints from Brazil and Mexico;
  - analyst "overdone" calls (Goldman, TIKR);
  - a stable BRL and good Latin American credit news.
- **Downside:**
  - a break below the 1,347.78 low, since there is no earnings catalyst until February 2027;
  - more analyst target cuts or downgrades (the 2027 estimate remains a soft spot);
  - Brazil credit deterioration or a weak Brazil macro or FX move;
  - competitor promotion headlines (Shopee, Amazon);
  - broad risk-off, because the stock behaved as high-beta on Nov 5.
- **Bottom line.** This is a sentiment and technical bounce setup, not a fundamental catalyst. The fundamentals are strong growth with margin compression and cheap valuation. The next hard datapoint is far off.

**DIA research, 9:00 AM CT Fri 2026-11-20: the Dow's slide is mostly a UnitedHealth and rates story, and a bounce is plausible but unconfirmed**

I ran 9 searches and opened 9 pages. Two returned nothing usable: the Fed minutes PDF (binary, no text) and the Zacks page (bot block). The secondary pages are mostly Mitrade, FXStreet and AP, plus the Fed minutes coverage in ADN, and they disagree on some figures. I found no Nov 19 close and no Nov 20 premarket or intraday coverage.

**The story**
- **The Dow has lost five sessions in a row.** On Nov 18 it fell to just above 50,000, its lowest in over three months, and is about 8% below its August high near 54,750. The S&P 500 also fell five straight sessions to about 7,325, its longest losing run since June. The Nasdaq 100 rose on Nov 18.
- **UnitedHealth (UNH) is the main idea-specific driver.** On Nov 16 CMS proposed the CRUSH rule, which would extend Medicare Advantage audits back to 2018 and apply sampled findings to whole plans. CMS puts recoveries at about $9B per payment year.
  - UNH fell about 5% on Nov 17 and about 10% on Nov 18, with Humana down 13%.
  - UNH is about 4.0% of DIA per State Street (SSGA), and about 4.3% of the Dow in FXStreet and Mitrade, whose weight appears to be a day older. Because the Dow is price-weighted, UNH explained about two-fifths of the Nov 18 point drop.
  - The rule is only proposed, comments are due Jan 19, 2027, and Oppenheimer expects legal challenges. Most savings would come from clawbacks in 2028-2030. This could ease, but it could also keep pressure on insurers.
- **Rates are the broad headwind.**
  - The Fed minutes, released Nov 18, show nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike at the Dec 8-9 meeting. CME FedWatch puts the odds near 95%.
  - Waller has argued for a half-point hike, and Musalem expects several hikes before spring 2027.
  - The 10-year Treasury yield was about 5.10-5.15% on Nov 17. Home Depot (down 2.4% on Nov 17) cited mortgage rates above 7%.
  - Oil is high: Brent was about $93 on Nov 17, with the Iran war unresolved.
- **Other Dow members have been weak.**
  - Nov 17: JPMorgan fell 2.4%, Disney 1.5%, Home Depot 2.4% or more.
  - Nov 18: Chevron fell almost 4% and Caterpillar over 2%.
  - Nvidia (Dow member) beat on revenue ($115.8B) and guided to $130B. The stock still fell about 3% on Nov 18, its fifth straight loss, and it carries a Jensen Huang CEO-succession story.
  - Salesforce lost more than 8% on Nov 17.
- **Dow versus S&P 500.** Early November was a rotation out of AI tech into banks and cyclicals. On Nov 4 the Dow gained 3.03% to 53,356 against 1.58% for the S&P, and Mitrade called it a rotation rather than a breakout. Since then the Dow has given it all back, and the Dow's decline is now deeper than the S&P's. This week the Dow's losses came from non-tech names plus UNH, so it is not a simple tech-versus-value story. The Dow lost 1.6% on Nov 17 against 1.0% for the S&P, and 1.1% on Nov 18 against 0.2%.
- **DIA composition.** The top weights are Goldman Sachs 10.25%, Caterpillar 6.5%, Microsoft 6.0%, Amgen 5.3%, Visa 4.9%, Travelers 4.7%, Apple 4.2%, Sherwin-Williams 4.1%, Home Depot 4.1% and UNH 4.0%. Financials are 27.5%, tech 18.1%, health care 14.2% and industrials 13.3%. The expense ratio is 0.16%. Single-stock moves in high-priced names drive the fund.

**What could move DIA over the next 1-10 sessions**
- **Technical levels.** The Dow's 200-day EMA is near 50,900, and its Nov 17 close was the first below it since late July. Wednesday's high briefly cleared it. Reclaiming and holding it would support a mean-reversion bounce, while failing leaves 50,000 and then lower. DIA's own 200-day average is 505.42.
- **UNH and insurers.** Watch for any CMS clarification, UnitedHealth's promised 2027 outlook (due before year-end) and legal pushback. UNH is oversold after two heavy down days, so a bounce would help DIA. More Humana, Elevance or CVS weakness would hurt.
- **Fed and yields.** Hike pricing is already near full, so the risk is a half-point or hawkish repricing. Fed speakers and any inflation data matter, and a 10-year yield above 5.15% would pressure the fund. The Fed decision on Dec 9 falls outside the window.
- **AI and tech.** The Anthropic listing on Nasdaq on Nov 19 (reported at $83, above its range) and Nvidia's follow-through matter for Microsoft, Apple and risk sentiment.
- **Oil and Iran headlines.** Moves in oil hit Chevron and airlines, and add to inflation worries.
- **Today's setup.** DIA is up 0.4% while SPY is down 0.4%, on volume running 2.1 times normal. That reads as value and defensive names catching a bid, or an oversold bounce, but I could not verify what drove it. The risk is that it is a dead-cat bounce inside a rate-driven downtrend, with the Dow still 8% off its high and under both its 50-day and 200-day averages.

**DaVita (DVA), research as of 9:00 AM CT Fri 2026-11-20**

I ran 9 searches and opened 7 sources in full: the Q3 8-K press release, the 10-Q, MarketBeat, Simply Wall St, StockStory, IBTimes and the Barchart article on Berkshire. The Barchart page came back empty, the Roic transcript returned a 403 error, and the 10-Q excerpt cut off before legal proceedings and risk factors. I found no 8:55 AM tape or news for today.

**The story**
- **August high, then a reset.** DVA hit 247.49 on Aug 3, then fell about 17% after Q2 results on margin doubts (the Simply Wall St headline said "17% sell off"). It has been drifting lower since.
- **Q3 report on Oct 29 was a beat that the market sold.**
  - Adjusted EPS was $3.82 against a $3.57 consensus. Revenue was $3.578B, up 4.6% from a year earlier.
  - Adjusted EPS fell from $4.02 in Q2. Adjusted operating income was $561M, a 15.7% margin.
  - Cost per treatment rose to $280.22 from $277.40, and revenue per treatment slipped $0.62 to $415.25.
  - Technology spending grew more than 20%, medical supply costs rose, and one source cites higher professional liability costs.
  - A $62M China impairment was excluded from adjusted results.
  - The stock closed at 193.31 before the report, then opened at 175.00 and traded around 178.84, down about 7%, on Oct 30 (MarketBeat). That is a bigger drop than the roughly 3% some summaries cite.
- **Guidance was only nudged.**
  - The low end of adjusted operating income rose to $2,175–2,250M.
  - Adjusted EPS is now $14.30–15.20 (midpoint about $14.75). Free cash flow is unchanged at $1.0–1.25B.
  - Integrated Kidney Care (IKC) is now expected to deliver at least $65M, ahead of plan.
  - U.S. treatment volume was up 1.2% year over year and normalized non-acquired growth was 0.4%.
  - Management called the finalized 2027 CMS (Medicare) payment rule a net positive but is still assessing it.
  - IT spending growth is expected to slow but not reverse. Dialyzer and AI benefits are not expected until 2028 or later.
- **Policy overhang.** On Oct 20 HHS issued its Kidney Care National Plan. It aims to lower barriers for new dialysis providers, expand home dialysis and spur competition. DaVita said the plan "reflects many of DaVita's priorities" but disputed that scale stands in the way of innovation. I could not verify the stock's reaction that day.
- **Berkshire is a supply source.** Under the 2024 repurchase agreement, Berkshire sold 382,563 shares at about $180.43 on Oct 27, about $69M, leaving 28.3M shares. Reports say it sold 1.2–1.6M shares per quarter earlier in 2026. The IBTimes article does not link the sale to any news.
- **Legal noise.** Several plaintiff firms (Pomerantz and others) announced investigations into whether government-policy and competition risks were disclosed. These are advertisements for potential claims, not lawsuits. I found no Lowey Dannenberg item, so a Benzinga/aggregator note on it is unconfirmed.
- **Buyback support.** DaVita repurchased 0.5M shares for $87M at an average of $180.57 from Oct 1 to Oct 27, and repurchased 2.2M shares for $348M in Q2. About 62.9M shares are outstanding, and the company is a steady buyer on dips.
- **Analysts.** Consensus is "Moderate Buy" with an average target of about $233, from four Buy and three Hold ratings. I could not find any target changes since Q3. The ratings I found date from July and August: Deutsche Bank and TD Cowen upgrades, UBS to $270, and Truist to $215 with a hold.

**Price context**
- One Benzinga-sourced figure has DVA closing at 173.00 on Nov 17. That is about 7.5% down over the month and roughly 26% below the August high.
- Your screen's 160.62 is about 7% below that, and it is a fresh low versus the post-earnings 175–178 area.
- I found no explanation for the slide from about 173 to about 156. The likeliest drivers are the HHS plan overhang, Berkshire and plaintiff-firm headlines, and selling pressure after a weak reaction to earnings. That is inference, not something I confirmed.
- Treat the price figures as approximate, since the sources conflict.

**What could move the stock over the next 1–10 sessions**
- **No scheduled company catalyst.** The next report is about Feb 1, 2027, so there is no earnings event inside the window.
- **Upside:**
  - Mean reversion from oversold levels (RSI 30, 3.4 ATR below its 20-day average).
  - Continued buybacks, which the company has been doing around 180 and presumably wants more of at 160.
  - Positive sell-side notes, since the fundamentals were not broken (EPS beat, guidance low end raised, IKC ahead).
  - Any evidence that the HHS plan is slow or modest in practice.
- **Downside:**
  - Further Berkshire sales (quarterly Form 4 filings) or more law-firm announcements.
  - HHS or CMS policy headlines on dialysis competition and home dialysis.
  - Broader healthcare or market weakness.
  - Lack of buyers: the stock is below both its 50-day (180.98) and 200-day (181.81) averages, and the bounce is on very light volume.

**Read:** The business story is intact but margin-limited, and the drop looks sentiment- and overhang-driven rather than tied to new bad fundamentals. A short-term oversold bounce is plausible. The window has no company catalyst, and light-volume strength at 25 minutes into the session is weak confirmation. I could not identify the cause of the 173-to-160 slide, so treat it as an unexplained move.

- Revenue was $611.1M, down 1.0% y/y, at the midpoint of the $607–615M guide.
- Adjusted EPS was $1.48, matching consensus of about $1.47. It sits inside the $1.43–1.53 guide.

- AI Pods (Globant's subscription AI delivery product) reached a $106.6M annualized run rate. That is double the $52.8M in June and up from $11.3M a year ago. The year-end target rose to at least $130M, from at least $110M.

- The $59.7M restructuring program is now complete. Headcount is 26,164, down from 29,020.
- Net debt is roughly $258M excluding leases. Q3 free cash flow was roughly $77M by my arithmetic, not a reported figure.

**What disappointed**
- Q4 revenue guidance is $596–604M, against consensus of about $610M. That is a decline of 1.4–2.7% y/y. Full-year revenue was narrowed to $2.429–2.437B, which cuts the August top end of $2.462B.
- The Middle East (the "new markets" segment) fell 34% y/y to $27.9M, and management expects no recovery in Q4. Excluding it, group growth was about +1.5%.
- Travel and hospitality revenue stepped down on high oil prices.
- Large accounts are converting to outcome-based pricing slowly. Smaller accounts are being pruned.
- Customers over $100K in trailing revenue fell to 882, from 978.
- Management gave no 2027 view and will do so in February. Q1 is usually seasonally soft.

- In August the company cut its guide, and the stock fell about 14% after hours. The 52-week low of 27.56 came in June, the lowest since 2017, amid fears that AI erodes IT-services demand.

  - Adjusted EPS is $2.29–$2.34, cut from $2.35–$2.45 and below the $2.35 consensus.

- The profit beat, Old Navy returning to flat, the Gap brand strength, the dividend raise and low inventory were all positives.

- The stock closed Thursday at 219.88, down 3.4%, before the report. After hours it fell about 5% to 7%, to roughly 205 to 209. The reports conflict.

- New Northeast stores are opening at 70% to 75% of chain-average volume, against the historical 60% to 65% assumption.
- Every major category had positive comps. Cosmetics and home were the strongest.
- Management sees no competitive pricing pressure. It expects peers that raised prices after tariffs to drift back toward Ross's pricing.
